questions.question_text: Does the word hold a foundational position relative to other inner-being characteristics — does it govern, generate, or organise them?

findings.session_b_note: Yes — the data provides a convergent answer from multiple angles. Gal 5:22 (OBS-103-128): love heads the singular fruit-of-Spirit list; the singularity of 'fruit' (not 'fruits') implies love as the one thing of which joy, peace, patience, etc. are expressions. 1Cor 13:13: 'the greatest of these is love' — ranked above faith and hope. Mat 22:37-40: all the Law and Prophets hang on the two love commandments — love organises the entire moral law. 1Jo 4:19: all human love flows from divine love — love is the causal origin of every other love-act. The data consistently positions love not as one virtue among others but as the virtue that organises, generates, and ranks the others. DIM-103-001 is resolved by this answer: love's 'inner-being architecture' is one where love governs all other relational dispositions. Lifecycle note: DIM-103-001 resolved via Q&A-142.

questions.question_text: Where the word has distinct modes of operation, are those modes held simultaneously or do they operate sequentially?
questions.review_note: supersession REVERSED 2026-06-14 — has Session-B findings; defer to the Session-B->L2 migration (element covered by T1.4.1)

findings.session_b_note: Both patterns appear in the data. Simultaneous: Exo 34:6 (OBS-103-069) — God is simultaneously rachum AND channun AND erek-appayim AND rab-chesed AND emet — five love-modes co-present as one divine character. Lam 3:22 (OBS-103-088) — chesed AND rachamim named together. Song 5:2 (OBS-103-108) — the beloved is simultaneously sister, love, dove, perfect one — multiple love-names applied simultaneously. Sequential: 1Jo 4:19 — divine love first, then human love in response (sequential). 1Pe 1:22 — obedience → purification → sincere love (sequential formation). Rom 5:5 → Gal 5:22 — Spirit infusion → fruit production (sequential). The data does not resolve to a single pattern — love's modes cohere simultaneously in their full expression (the divine portrait) and arise sequentially in their human formation.

questions.question_text: Does the word have an inherent directionality — is it always oriented toward an object — and what does the choice of object determine about the word's moral character?

findings.session_b_note: Yes — love is always directed. The grammar confirms this: agapaō always takes a direct object; the philo-compound system is entirely object-defining (love-of-X where X determines the compound). No instance of undirected love appears in the data — love is constitutively directional (OBS-103-017, OBS-103-009). The object determines love's moral character entirely: the inner mechanism is identical whether the object is God (filotheos — morally ordered) or pleasure (filēdonos — morally disordered) or money (filarguros). This is the data's most consistently evidenced structural feature: the same inner act of attachment produces radically different moral outcomes based solely on the object. The moral life in the biblical data is substantially a question of love's direction — not whether one loves but what one loves. This confirms L-004's anticipated finding (below).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-002: Love's definition as directed-attachment-toward-an-object generates a characteristic pattern of faculty engagement. Because love is always toward an object, it necessarily engages attention (what is a…
findings.finding_value: Love's definition as directed-attachment-toward-an-object generates a characteristic pattern of faculty engagement. Because love is always toward an object, it necessarily engages attention (what is attended to is the beloved — Phili 4:8), reason (judgment of the object's worth and the hierarchy of competing loves — Mat 10:37), memory (remembering the beloved sustains love — Jer 31:20), and identity (what is loved constitutes who one is — Q&A-075). The definition's object-determination principle (moral quality determined by object) maps onto the moral sensitivity faculty: the faculty that calibrates moral perception is calibrated by love's direction — you notice what you love, and what you love as most important determines what you register as morally significant (Psa 97:10 — love-of-God generates hate-of-evil). The definition's tripartite structure (disposition/act/condition) maps onto the faculty architecture: disposition engages the will and conscience; act engages the relational capacity and body; condition engages identity and emotion. No faculty operates independently of love's fundamental structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-003: Love's definition as directed attachment reaches its relational specification in T4's three-axis architecture. The object-determination principle (Q&A-144) — that love's moral quality depends entirely…
findings.finding_value: Love's definition as directed attachment reaches its relational specification in T4's three-axis architecture. The object-determination principle (Q&A-144) — that love's moral quality depends entirely on its object — is enacted relationally when the proper objects are named: God (vertical-ascending), neighbour and enemy (horizontal), and the beloved community (horizontal-mutual). The definition's three registers map onto the relational axes: the dispositional register (stable inner orientation) grounds the covenantal-faithful love in the GOD→HUMAN axis (God's chesed never ceasing — Lam 3:22); the active register (commanded, exercised) grounds the love of neighbour and enemy (Lev 19:18, Mat 5:44); the condition register (being-loved as identity) is the GOD→HUMAN axis's effect in the person (agapētos — constituted as beloved). The relational interfaces reveal what the definition describes abstractly: love's mechanism in concrete directional operation. The most significant inter-tier finding: the definition's requirement that love be directed toward an object is fulfilled eschatologically when the object is perfectly and permanently God — Jer 31:34, 1Jo 4:18 (perfect love).

questions.question_text: Can the word function as an identity diagnostic — does what a person does with this word reveal what kind of person they are?

findings.session_b_note: Yes — this is one of the data's most strongly evidenced structural claims. 2Ti 3:2-4 (OBS-103-137) lists philautos (self-lover) and philēdonos (pleasure-lover) vs filotheos (God-lover) as the diagnostic markers distinguishing the last-days person from the faithful person. Joh 3:19 (OBS-103-147): 'people loved the darkness' — the love-choice is the diagnostic of judgment. Joh 13:35 (OBS-103-129): 'by this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another' — the community's love-practice is the external diagnostic of their identity. Mat 10:37 (OBS-103-151): whoever loves father or mother more than Christ 'is not worthy of me' — the hierarchy of love is the diagnostic of worthiness. What a person loves is not merely a preference — it is a revelation of what they are. The love-diagnostic is both internal (self-knowledge) and external (publicly legible community identity).

questions.question_text: Does the word operate at a level below conscious attention or deliberate will — and if so, what does this imply about its depth in the inner being?

findings.session_b_note: Yes — the data provides evidence of love operating below the threshold of deliberate conscious attention. Song 5:2 (OBS-103-108): 'I slept, but my heart was awake' — love-awareness persists in sleep, below waking consciousness. 1Ki 3:26 (OBS-103-105): the mother's rachamim for her son is described as physiological movement (nichmeruh — heated, turbulent) — an involuntary somatic response. Jer 31:20 (OBS-103-117): God's inner parts 'hamu' (murmur, are agitated) for Ephraim — the movement of the inner organs is described as spontaneous, not deliberate. The compassion-movement (splanchnizō, Luk 15:20) triggers before deliberate action (running, embracing). These instances suggest love has a pre-reflective dimension — an inner orienting toward the beloved that is already present before the person consciously engages it. Implication: love is not fully within the person's deliberate control at its deepest level; it is constitutive of the inner person at a depth below ordinary conscious access.

questions.question_text: Does the vocabulary of the word include a systematic taxonomy of its own misdirected forms — and if so, what structural logic organises that taxonomy?

findings.session_b_note: Yes — the philo-compound disordered forms constitute a taxonomy (OBS-103-036, OBS-103-017): filarguria/filarguros (love of money — 3 groups), filēdonos (love of pleasure), filoneikia/filoneikos (love of dispute), filoprōteuō (love of being first), filia tou kosmou (friendship with world — Jam 4:4), agapaō-darkness/world (Joh 3:19, 2Ti 4:10), agavah (lust — H5691), filautos (love of self — 2Ti 3:2). The structural logic organising the taxonomy: all disordered loves are the same inner mechanism (directed attachment) applied to one of three wrong object-classes: (a) **Material objects** — money, pleasure; (b) **Social-positional objects** — primacy, dispute-victory; (c) **The self** — self-love, friendship with the world as self-assertion. The taxonomy is not arbitrary — it maps the full range of objects that compete with God and the neighbour as the proper objects of love. The disordered loves are a systematic counter-ordering of the inner person's relational architecture.

questions.question_text: Does the word have a definitional outward expression — a form that constitutes what the word is rather than merely evidencing it?

findings.session_b_note: Yes — the data names two constitutive outward expressions: (a) **Self-giving** — Joh 15:13 (OBS-103-125): 'greater love has no one than this: to lay down one's life for one's friends.' The self-giving is not the evidence of love — it is love's maximum constitutive form. The act constitutes the love at its greatest — without the self-giving there is no greater love, only a lesser form. (b) **Obedience** — Joh 14:15: 'if you love me, you will keep my commandments.' Commandment-keeping is not merely love's fruit — it is love's definitive form toward Christ. The absence of commandment-keeping in the professed lover of Christ constitutes a question about whether the love is genuine. The kiss (filēma, katafileō) is also a constitutive rather than merely evidential act — the Judas-kiss (Luk 22:48) is dangerous precisely because it uses love's constitutive act to signal the opposite.

questions.question_text: Is the word named in Scripture as constitutive of the divine essence — what God is — rather than merely as a divine attribute or act?
questions.review_note: supersession REVERSED 2026-06-14 — has Session-B findings; defer to the Session-B->L2 migration (element covered by T0.1.1+T0.3.2)

findings.session_b_note: Yes — explicitly in 1Jo 4:8 ('God is love — ho theos agapē estin') and 1Jo 4:16 ('God is love'). The predicate nominative construction in Greek (theos agapē) makes love not a description of what God does but an identification of what God is. This is the programme's most significant theological claim: love is not one of God's attributes among others but the identification of God's being. The data also evidences this from the OT side: Song 8:6 (OBS-103-096) names love's flame as 'the very flame of the Lord' (shalhevetyah) — love's intensity is grounded in the divine name. Exo 34:6 (OBS-103-069) names love/chesed as the first and most prominent of God's proclaimed attributes. The NT claim (God is love) has OT preparation in the priority of chesed in the divine self-characterisation.

questions.question_text: Does the word's structural opposite operate under the same moral logic as the word itself — can the contrary also be either rightly or wrongly directed?

findings.session_b_note: Yes — and the data makes this explicit. Psa 97:10 (OBS-103-115): 'O you who love the Lord, hate evil' — hatred of evil is commanded of those who love God. Righteous hatred is not love's failure but love's necessary complement: you cannot love God and be indifferent to what opposes him. Lev 19:17 (OBS-103-114): 'you shall not hate your brother in your heart' — hatred of the brother is wrong. The same inner-being mechanism (hatred as directed-aversion) can be rightly directed (at evil) or wrongly directed (at the brother). This is the precise structural parallel to love: love rightly directed (toward God and neighbour) vs love wrongly directed (toward money, pleasure, world). Hatred operates under the same moral logic as love: the mechanism is morally neutral; the object determines the moral quality. The ordered inner life requires both rightly directed love AND rightly directed hatred.

questions.question_text: What is the relationship between the word as an inner disposition and the word as an outward act — are they competitors, co-expressions, or in a different structural relationship?

findings.session_b_note: The data positions them in a **generative relationship** — disposition generates act. The chesed that is written on the heart (Pro 3:3, OBS-103-090) is the disposition that produces the acts of Ruth's chesed (Rut 3:10, OBS-103-089) and the acts of social kindness in the neighbour-relationships. Love of Christ as inner disposition produces commandment-keeping as outward act (Joh 14:15, OBS-103-140). The compassion-movement (inner) produces running, embracing, kissing (outer) in Luk 15:20 (OBS-103-057). The relationship is not competitive (as if outer act were less genuine than inner disposition) nor merely co-present (as if they were unrelated). Disposition and act are related as inner origin and outer expression — the act is the disposition's actualisation in a specific relational moment. 1Ki 8:18 (OBS-103-103) confirms: God accepts the inner disposition (it was in your heart) even when the act is not performed — the disposition has value prior to and independent of the act. But the disposition that never produces an act is not evidenced as genuine love in the data — love without expression is not thematised as sufficient.

questions.question_text: Does the word carry an epistemic dimension — is knowing and being known a structural component of the word's operation?

findings.session_b_note: Yes — the epistemic dimension of love is one of the data's most distinctive findings. Joh 15:15 (OBS-103-052): love's definitive act is knowledge-disclosure — Jesus names the friends as those to whom he has made known all that he heard from the Father. The friend-love relationship is constituted by mutual knowledge-sharing. Hos 6:6 (OBS-103-091): 'knowledge of God' (da'at elohim) co-prioritised with chesed — love and knowing are structural companions in the OT. Jer 31:34 (OBS-103-072): in the new covenant, each person will know God directly — the eschatological love-community is one of immediate knowledge. Joh 21:17 (OBS-103-153): Peter's love-confession appeals to Christ's omniscience ('Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you') — being known by Christ is the ground of the love-confession. The epistemic dimension: love is the relational structure within which knowing becomes possible; knowledge is what love shares; being known is the most intimate expression of being loved.

questions.question_text: Does the word function as a publicly legible signal — a means by which something about the inner community or person is read by those outside?

findings.session_b_note: Already addressed at T4.5.2 (Q&A-088) and multiple points. Yes — Joh 13:35 ('by this all people will know') is the primary evidence. The community's mutual love is publicly legible to 'all people' (pantas) — it functions as the community's primary external sign. The individual's love-choices (what they love) also function publicly as identity diagnostics (2Ti 3:2-4 list is observable; the Pharisees' money-love was observable — Luk 16:14). Love is both internally real (inner disposition) and externally readable (community sign and individual identity marker). No additional findings beyond prior Q&A responses.

questions.question_text: Does the word produce a reorganisation of social dynamics — and if so, in what direction does it reorganise them?

findings.session_b_note: Yes — and the data names the direction explicitly. The reorganisation operates in three directions: (a) **Restructuring of kinship** — Mat 12:50 (OBS-103-063): the family is restructured around shared orientation toward God rather than natural kinship. Love's community replaces the natural family as the primary social unit. (b) **Inversion of competitive hierarchy** — Rom 12:10 (OBS-103-119): 'outdo one another in showing honor' — the social competition is reversed from honour-claiming to honour-giving. Love reorganises from rivalry to generosity. (c) **Inclusion of the excluded** — Mat 5:44 (OBS-103-143): enemy-love includes those whom natural social dynamics exclude. The direction of love's social reorganisation is consistently: from exclusion toward inclusion, from taking toward giving, from natural kinship toward chosen community. The community constituted by love (Joh 13:35) is a social body organised on principles that invert the natural social order.
